- If sentiment shows strong bullish momentum (e.g., >0.67 for multiple days) and forecast is rising steadily, reduce forecast slope slightly to avoid over-optimism.  
- If sentiment turns bearish (e.g., <0.00 or negative spikes) and forecast is still rising, cut forecast peak early to prevent overshoot.  
- When true outcome shows sharp reversal after a spike, model often overcorrects — reduce forecast slope after peak and add slight downward bias.  
- If recent history shows mean reversion (e.g., 3–5 days of price decline after peak), model should not assume continuation — adjust forecast to reflect mean-reversion bias.  
- If sentiment is mixed or neutral (e.g., 0.33–0.67) and forecast is flat, consider slight upward bias to account for latent bullish sentiment.  
- Avoid forecasting linear trends when sentiment shows volatility — use smoothing or stepwise adjustments based on sentiment swing direction.  
- If forecast is consistently higher than true outcome over 3–5 days, reduce forecast by 1–2% per day to reflect underestimation bias.  
- If forecast is consistently lower than true outcome, increase forecast by 1–2% per day to reflect overestimation bias — especially if sentiment is bullish.
